dedupe_keys.name: hydro quebec blackout in the march 1989 geomagnetic storm

description: This case study covers the blackout of the Hydro-Québec power system at 2:44 a.m. on 13 March 1989, during the largest magnetic storm of the twentieth century, as described by Hydro-Québec, the Natural Resources Canada space weather chronology and a 2019 re-analysis by D. H. Boteler in Space Weather. Geomagnetically induced currents on the long 735 kV lines crossing the Canadian Shield caused harmonics and voltage asymmetry, seven static var compensators tripped in turn, all five lines to Montréal lost synchronism, and the 21,000 MW grid collapsed in 25 seconds, leaving Québec dark for more than nine hours. Boteler traced the storm to two coronal mass ejections, from an X4.5 flare on 10 March and an M7.3 flare on 12 March, and found that the substorm hit at the second storm sudden commencement, early in the storm; later, lower-latitude disturbances affected power systems in the United States, the United Kingdom and Sweden. Hydro-Québec then recalibrated protection, added a real-time disturbance alert system, changed operating procedures during storms and installed series compensation on lines. The Hydro-Québec page is accessible online as free HTML, and the chronology is on spaceweather.gc.ca. Caveats: customer numbers and costs are not given on these sources, and the paper is not open access. It illustrates post-event analysis of space weather hazard exposure and cascading failure in a power grid; related records are SuperMAG, OMNIWeb and the NRCan space weather effects chronology.
